extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in pragmatics, cognitive science, and humor studies
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing or designing humorous utterances/events by identifying and manipulating metarepresentations (representations of representations) that hearers construct; ties to theory-of-mind capacity and relevance-theoretic pragmatics. Useful for scholars, analysts, and writers who want a cognitive-pragmatic account of how humor is produced and perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: At least one metarepresentation is being constructed
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one metarepresentation is being constructed by the hearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A metarepresentation is a representation of a representation (e.g., 'He thinks that p', 'She believes that he believes that q'). Humor requires the hearer to model a character's/speaker's belief, attitude, or utterance as a representation rather than just processing surface content.

rubrics_metrics.name: A contrasting representation (or reality) exists
rubrics_metrics.description: A second representation (or reality) contrasts with the metarepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical setup: the hearer constructs 'the character believes X' while simultaneously holding 'in fact not-X'. The contrast between the attributed belief and actual state is the source of comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous holding of both representations
rubrics_metrics.description: The hearer simultaneously holds both the metarepresentation and the contrasting representation with sufficient cognitive grip to perceive the contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor depends on the hearer's capacity to entertain both representations at once rather than collapsing one into the other; timing and presentation must support this cognitive simultaneousness (e.g., through dramatic irony or narrative pacing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affective outcome: enjoyment rather than distress
rubrics_metrics.description: The hearer enjoys, rather than is distressed by, the contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contrast must be perceived as amusing. If the discrepancy produces fear, sadness, or threat, it will not function as humor under this account. Designers should calibrate stakes and audience sensitivity to avoid distress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of metarepresentation required
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify what order of metarepresentation (1st, 2nd, 3rd, etc.) the humorous interpretation requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher-order cases (e.g., irony, sarcasm) require the hearer to represent beliefs about beliefs (e.g., 'She believes that he believes that p'). Higher-order metarepresentations demand greater theory-of-mind sophistication and affect which audience segments can appreciate the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience theory-of-mind capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor depends on the hearer's theory-of-mind capacities; without ToM, many forms of humor are inaccessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictions: children acquire humor capacities in step with ToM milestones; individuals on the autism spectrum may show altered humor profiles (less appreciation of social-deceptive humor, intact appreciation of structural humor). Account for developmental and population differences when designing or evaluating humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design: choose a character whose beliefs the audience can model
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a character whose beliefs the audience can clearly model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the character's perspective or epistemic state salient and easy to attribute (clear cues, consistent behavior, recognizable role). If the audience cannot build a reliable metarepresentation of the character, the intended comic contrast will fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design: set up a discrepancy between character belief and audience knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up a discrepancy between character belief and audience knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engineer situations where the audience knows information the character lacks (dramatic irony), or where the character's inference is predictably wrong. The explicit mismatch is the locus of the joke; use context, staging, or narrator hints to create it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design: maintain the discrepancy long enough
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain the discrepancy long enough for the audience to feel its weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing matters: sustain the audience's dual representations sufficiently for them to detect and savor the contrast, but avoid overextension that reduces surprise or clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design: trigger the moment of perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Trigger the moment of perception of the contrast—often via dramatic irony, narrator hint, or character action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an explicit cue, punchline, or event that makes the audience recognize the mismatch between beliefs and reality. The trigger converts a latent discrepancy into a perceived contrast that yields amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude stimuli that produce no metarepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Stimuli that produce no metarepresentation (purely structural surprises with no agent) are excluded from this account of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purely formal or structural incongruities that do not prompt modeling of an agent's belief/attitude will not be explained as metarepresentational humor. Recognize this anti-pattern when analyzing 'jokes' that rely only on pattern violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude stimuli beyond audience metarepresentational reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Stimuli where the audience can't reach the required metarepresentational level (audience's ToM capacity insufficient) are excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a joke requires second- or third-order belief attribution but the target audience lacks those ToM skills, the joke will fail; consider audience developmental or cognitive profile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude discrepancies that cause distress rather than amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrepancies that cause distress rather than amusement (the contrast feels threatening or sad) are excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the perceived mismatch evokes negative affect (threat, grief, humiliation), the metarepresentational structure produces non-humorous outcomes; designers should avoid elevating stakes that shift affect away from amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic questions for analyzing humorous interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of diagnostic questions to apply when evaluating whether an utterance/event produces metarepresentational humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: What metarepresentation does the joke ask the hearer to construct? What is the contrasting representation/reality? Is the audience capable of holding both simultaneously? Does the hearer enjoy the contrast, or does it produce some other affect? What order of metarepresentation (1st, 2nd, 3rd) is required?

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-order metarepresentational humor types (irony, sarcasm, misattributed belief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony, sarcasm, and misattributed-belief comedies are higher-order cases that rely on metarepresentations of attributed voices or attitudes and the speaker's dissociation from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony: speaker attributes an utterance and dissociates from it; Sarcasm: speaker metarepresents a critical attitude toward someone who would say X; Misattributed belief comedy: audience watches characters acting on false beliefs the audience knows to be false. These forms demand more complex attribution and clearer cues to speaker stance.
